fields.question: Why add landmarks beyond the local ULTRA-HSTU window?
fields.answer: Local attention preserves detail; sparse landmarks connect distant behavior. LBSL widens deeper layers. Sparse access is not lossless full-HSTU equivalence.
fields.example: Read recent events individually and use representative remote positions.

fields.question: How do semi-local attention and deeper wider windows differ from one fixed window?
fields.answer: Deeper layers gain wider direct access, while fixed windows retain identical local connections per layer. Effective reach also depends on stacking and landmarks; one formula does not cover mixture, precision, and systems changes.
fields.example: Read a visit closely in shallow layers, then relate cross-visit interests deeper.

fields.question: Can a 48-event ablation prove the 16K production scaling law?
fields.answer: No. It lacks 18-layer production models, dynamic topology, FP8 kernels, and private logs. Scaling needs matched runs across lengths and hardware measurement.
fields.example: A max-length setting of 16000 does not test long history if only dozens are loaded.

fields.question: Why combine local windows, landmarks, and increasing layer reach?
fields.answer: Fixed local masks lose remote paths and full attention is expensive. Sparse landmarks provide global connections, wider deeper windows integrate more context, and mixture/system changes support scale. Efficiency depends on windows, landmark counts, and kernels.
fields.example: Shallow layers read recent clicks, while landmarks and deeper layers connect older interests without recovering every event.

fields.question: Why tokenize feature roles and tasks in UniFormer?
fields.answer: One interaction interface carries candidate-independent, candidate-dependent, and task-specific states. Tokenization preserves role distinctions rather than flattening all fields.
fields.example: User history, current product, and click objective each get appropriate tokens.

fields.question: What is the trade-off versus separate models per task?
fields.answer: Shared interactions can transfer signal and ease maintenance; task tokens condition predictions. Parameter sharing can still cause interference.
fields.example: Viewing features may help clicks but conflict with commerce goals.

fields.question: How avoid token misalignment locally?
fields.answer: Match role, position, and valid mask to fields, and have each task head read its own state. MovieLens lacks industrial fields and serving.
fields.example: Task A reading task B's token is wrong despite matching shapes.

fields.question: Why distinguish candidate-independent, candidate-dependent, and task tokens before unified interactions?
fields.answer: They encode common user state, current match, and prediction objective respectively. Explicit roles ease scaling, but joint interactions can make states candidate-dependent; reuse needs masks and architecture.
fields.example: A shared age token is reusable, but a state containing one candidate's price is not.

fields.question: Why separate baseline click propensity and coupon-strength sensitivity?
fields.answer: Users may buy anyway. Separate natural propensity from treatment response to estimate increment rather than conversion under a coupon.
fields.example: A coupon used by someone who would buy anyway does not necessarily generate a sale.

fields.question: Why isn't treatment CTR uplift?
fields.answer: Uplift compares treated and untreated potential outcomes under matched conditions; high treated CTR can reflect selection. Counterfactual identification needs assumptions, not just two predictions.
fields.example: Coupons targeted to high-intent users can show high CTR without causing it.

fields.question: Does local UniMVT have randomized coupon tiers and counterfactuals?
fields.answer: No. MovieLens checks two-tower and counterfactual constraints only. Causal estimates require overlap and confounding control; test outcomes must not define treatment.
fields.example: Assigning coupons by rating leaks outcomes into group assignment.

fields.question: Why separate baseline and coupon sensitivity before comparing predictions?
fields.answer: Natural propensity can masquerade as coupon gain. Two towers model baseline/treatment; counterfactual constraints link unobserved cases, and unit uplift normalizes tier increments. Identification still depends on assignment and assumptions.
fields.example: A naturally 80%-likely buyer may gain less than one moving 20%→50%, subject to selection bias.

fields.question: Why use a flat UNIQUE code instead of residual levels?
fields.answer: It avoids stagewise quantization error, using feedback towers, frequency correction, and EMA for one level alongside retrieval and ranking losses. Flat codes need not uniquely identify items.
fields.example: Retrieve one semantic bucket, then rank its items.

fields.question: How does shared-prefix-only candidate attention differ from setwise attention?
fields.answer: Candidate isolation reuses user encoding and avoids peers changing scores. Setwise attention depends on the candidate set. Unified retrieval and ranking do not require item-to-item reads.
fields.example: Adding a candidate should not alter an existing candidate through peer attention.

fields.question: Do straight-through quantization and balanced code usage establish retrieval quality?
fields.answer: No. Straight-through preserves gradients and correction helps usage, not relevance. Three small seeds do not rebuild industrial indexes, P99, or online gains.
fields.example: Equally sized buckets can contain uniformly irrelevant mixtures.

fields.question: Why use flat codes and forbid candidates from reading each other?
fields.answer: Flat allocation avoids error accumulation and uses feedback, frequency correction, and EMA. Shared prefixes save user encoding; item/code isolation keeps scoring independent. Joint objectives connect retrieval and ranking; monitor use and collisions.
fields.example: Retrieve one-level code buckets and score each candidate against the same history, not its neighbors.

fields.question: Why use generated SID traces as a ranking bridge?
fields.answer: The generated path contains intermediate retrieval choices, beyond a shared encoder or final ID. A heterogeneous decoder reads the trace with item features.
fields.example: Rank with the semantic prefixes that led to the item.

fields.question: Why do generation and ranking queries need different masks?
fields.answer: Generation reads only earlier SIDs; ranking can read the full path and synchronized item tokens. Future code access would leak generation targets, while restricting ranking can hide useful evidence.
fields.example: Level-two generation cannot read level three, but ranking can.

fields.question: How does ranking LoRA protect the shared generation trunk?
fields.answer: Stop gradients through shared Q/K/V outputs in the ranking branch and train ranking-specific LoRA. This is not freezing everything or fully sharing gradients. Local scope excludes production beams and parallelism.
fields.example: Ranking loss changes LoRA without updating shared generation projections through that route.

fields.question: Why let ranking read SID traces but detach shared outputs and train LoRA?
fields.answer: Paths supply retrieval evidence. Role-specific masks share forward information, while detached shared outputs and low-rank updates reduce backward interference.
fields.example: Rank using outdoor→camping→tent while adjusting only ranking LoRA for new scoring preferences.

fields.question: Why keep two separate pre-ranking and ranking towers?
fields.answer: Their features, candidate scales, and latency differ. Share some embeddings and align downstream preference through training, without exposing expensive online ranking input upstream.
fields.example: Pre-ranking learns fine-ranker preference from supervision, not its full feature set.

fields.question: How does CPPA differ from majority-voting among objectives?
fields.answer: Opposing evidence contributes to two softplus terms rather than discarding the minority. CAPP chooses confident directed pairs and AGRR controls group drift separately.
fields.example: Clicks can prefer A and watch time B; retain both directions.

fields.question: How keep cross-stage gradient isolation and AGRR evidence separate from pruning?
fields.answer: Cross-stage alignment uses survivors and freezes the fine-ranker direction. AGRR builds grouped KL targets from unpruned inputs, not centered scores. Document variance and quantile ties.
fields.example: Computing evidence after pruning changes the distribution AGRR should see.

fields.question: Why preserve both directions for one pair in CPPA?
fields.answer: Objectives can disagree, and a majority loses strength and minority signal. Both softplus penalties remain, CAPP selects confident directions, and grouped KL limits drift. Downstream supervision is training-only.
fields.example: Clicks favor A while purchases favor B; majority voting can hide the purchase signal.

fields.question: Why generate an attribute chain before SIDs?
fields.answer: Explicit category, seller, and brand context can bridge generative and discriminative representations. The chain guides content and does not establish independent language reasoning.
fields.example: Generate category and brand before the detailed semantic path.
